I.

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

M.P.W., representing himself, seeks damages
arising out of an arrest by the police almost ten years ago. The case wound its
way to trial two years ago before Justice Butler but could not proceed because
of defective pleadings. Justice Butler struck significant aspects of the claim
but granted M.P.W. an opportunity to file an amended pleading – which M.P.W.
did on November 23, 2017 (“ANOCC”).

[
2
]

The defendants now apply pursuant to Rules
9-5(1)(b), (c) and (d) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, B.C. Reg.
115/2009 [the Rules] to strike the amended pleading without leave to amend or,
alternatively, that the plaintiff be required to seek leave of the court to
file any further amended pleadings.

[
3
]

On August 22, 2019, I granted the defendants’
application (with reasons to follow) to strike the ANOCC. I also granted an
order that the defendants be provided their costs of this application in any
event of the cause. At the same time, I granted leave to the plaintiff to file
a further amended notice of civil claim in the form filed on July 22, 2019,
subject to the revisions set out in the terms of the order I made on August 22,
2019.

[
4
]

These are my reasons for granting the orders.

II.

PLEADINGS CHRONOLOGY

[
5
]

This litigation has a long and protracted
history. I will set out some of the events relevant to this application. The
plaintiff filed a Notice of Civil Claim on November 30, 2012, wherein he
alleged a multiplicity of claims against the defendants arising out of his
arrest by members of the Victoria Police Department in November 2010. The
arrest occurred in circumstances where allegations of inappropriate sexual
conduct were raised by his then seven-year-old daughter (“V.W.”) to a
representative of the Ministry of Children and Family Development. In response
to the allegations and a report made to the Victoria Police, Det. Mark Knoop
was assigned to investigate. He interviewed V.W. on November 26, 2010, at the
Victoria Police Department. As a result of that interview, the plaintiff was
arrested (by the defendant, Cory Moore) without warrant on November 30, 2010,
for a sexual offence relating to his daughter. He was held and interviewed by the
police for about four hours and subsequently released on an undertaking. No
charges were ever laid against the plaintiff.

[
6
]

Two years after his arrest, the plaintiff filed
a notice of civil claim naming the City of Victoria, Mark Knoop, Cory Moore and
the Victoria Police Department. The claim contained allegations of false arrest
and false imprisonment, abuse of process, assault and battery, and defamation.

[
7
]

On December 21, 2012, the defendants filed their
response to notice of civil claim. In its written submission in this
application, the defendants provided a detailed summary of the events from December
2012 to September 2017. I will not repeat it here except to say this: The
plaintiff took virtually no steps to prosecute his claim from 2012–2015, to the
point that the defendants filed an application to dismiss for want of
prosecution on October 25, 2015. That application was ultimately determined by
Justice Jenkins on May 12, 2016, at which point he granted various orders,
including an order that a trial date be set by June 10, 2016. Pursuant to that
order, the plaintiff obtained a trial date of September 25, 2017.

[
8
]

In the spring and summer of 2017, the plaintiff
sent correspondence to the defendants that he intended to amend his claim
although he failed to take any steps to formally do so.

[
9
]

On September 12, 2017, the defendants filed an
application seeking an order striking the plaintiff’s notice of civil claim as
disclosing no reasonable claim against the defendants.

[
10
]

On the day the case was set for trial, Butler J. determined the
application to strike the notice of civil claim. Justice Butler granted that
order, dismissing all of the plaintiff’s claims. He also granted leave to the
plaintiff to file an amended notice of civil claim respecting some of the
dismissed allegations.

[
11
]

Justice Butler summarized the notice of civil
claim as follows:

The notice of
civil claim is very poorly drafted and makes some allegations of fact, although
much of it is a series of conclusory statements. I’ll give an example, and this
example really goes to the substance of [M.P.W.’s] claim... He states that the
Victoria police department used their authority in an improper purpose to
wrongfully, intentionally and maliciously arrest and detain [M.P.W.] where no
crime had been committed, and with intent to separate him from his daughter
without just cause. At the end of the notice of civil claim he alleges three
causes of action under the heading, “Legal Basis”, and those are the torts of
abuse of process, assault and battery, and defamation. (Lowe Affidavit #
9, Ex.
31, pp. 268
; BOD, p. 367).

[
12
]

At the conclusion of the application, Butler J.
ordered the following:

a)

All claims against the defendant, Victoria
Police Department, are dismissed, without leave to amend;

b)

All claims in defamation against Cory Moore, are
dismissed, without leave to amend;

c)

All tort claims in assault and battery, and
abuse of process are dismissed against all of the defendants, without leave to
amend;

d)

The notice of civil claim filed November 30,
2012 is struck pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
;
and

e)

The plaintiff is at liberty to file an amended
notice of civil claim within 60 days of September 26, 2017, which must be
limited to claims of (for the period of November 22, 2010 to January 14, 2011):

i.

Negligent investigation;

ii.

Wrongful arrest; and

iii.

Defamation, which, if made:

(1)

Must be limited to claims referred to in paragraph
1(j) of the NOCC, alleging defamatory statements made by the defendant, Mark
Knoop to one or more identified individual(s) at the Ministry of Children and
Family Development; and

(2)

Must be particularized, setting out the words of
the defamatory statements made, the timing of the statements, the mode of
communication, whether orally or in writing, and to whom the statements were
made;

[
13
]

On November 23, 2017, the plaintiff filed the ANOCC
pursuant to the order of Justice Butler. In their written submission, the
defendants described the ANOCC in this way:

The amended
pleading more than tripled the length of the original. Part 1 of the original
NOCC set out the facts in less than three pages, with one main paragraph
containing 21 sub-paragraphs. The ANOCC sets out the facts in approximately 12
pages, with one main paragraph containing 73 sub-paragraphs.

[
14
]

On April 3, 2019, the defendants filed an application to strike the
ANOCC. The defendants accommodated the plaintiff’s request (three times) to
adjourn the application to strike, on the basis that the plaintiff was either
unavailable and/or suffering from injuries sustained in an accident.

[
15
]

Ultimately, this application came before me on July 5, 2019. The
plaintiff was unable to conclude his submissions and a further hour was
scheduled for July 11, 2019. On July 11, 2019, the plaintiff submitted that he
had considered the defendants’ submissions and the deficiencies raised. In
response to those submissions, the plaintiff submitted that he had prepared a
further “document” taking into account those deficiencies. I granted his
request to deliver that document and granted leave to the defendants to respond
to it. Pursuant to my direction, the plaintiff delivered a proposed further
amended notice of civil claim on July 22, 2019 (“Further ANOCC”), asking that
it replace the ANOCC.

[
16
]

The defendants take the position that the ANOCC should be struck and
leave not be granted to amend pursuant to the Further ANOCC, or at all. The
plaintiff submits that he is self-represented, that he now understands the
requirements of pleadings, he has done his best to comply with Butler J.’s orders
and it is in the interests of justice that he should be allowed to proceed with
his claim as set out in the Further ANOCC.

III.

LAW

[
17
]

Rule 9-5(1) of the Rules states:

(1) At any stage of a proceeding, the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading,
petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be, [not relied on in this case]

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
18
]

The law related to striking pleadings was
summarized by Justice Voith in
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
at paras.
57–63
,
appeal dismissed as abandoned
2017 BCCA 96
:

[57] The test on an application to strike an
action under R. 9-5(1)(a), on the basis the pleadings do not disclose a cause
of action, is whether it is plain and obvious the claim cannot succeed. It
requires a conclusion that, assuming that the facts as stated are true, those
facts disclose no cause of action and the pleadings disclose no arguable issue.
If there is a chance that the action may succeed, then the action should be
allowed to proceed;
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959
at 980;
Thompson v. Webber
,
2010 BCCA 308
at para.
11
;
Canadian
Bar Assn. v. British Columbia
,
2008 BCCA 92
at para.
37
.

[58] The test for striking a pleading under
R. 9-5(1)(b), on the basis that it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious, was recently summarized in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC
1083
, where Fisher J. said:

[20] Under Rule
9-5(1)(b), a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff's cause of action, if it does not advance any claim
known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it
would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the court's time and
public resources:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish
Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (SC);
Skender v Farley
,
2007
BCCA 629
. If a pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what
is pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious.

[59] An "embarrassing" pleading,
as contemplated by R. 9-5(1)(c), is one that is so irrelevant that to allow it
to stand would involve useless expense and would also prejudice the trial of
the action by involving the parties in a dispute apart from the issues;
Keddie
v. Dumas Hotels Ltd
. (1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (C.A.).

[60] The abuse of process standard under R.
9-5(1)(d) derives from a flexible doctrine. It allows the court to prevent a
claim from proceeding where to do so would violate principles of judicial
economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of
justice;
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at paras.
35-37
.

[61] Though subsections (a)-(d) of R. 9-5(1)
address different concerns and different wrongs, there is also some overlap
between these subsections. Thus, for example, a pleading that discloses no
cause of action, contrary to R. 9-5(1)(a), can also be unnecessary, frivolous
or vexatious within the meaning of R. 9-5(1)(b); see e.g.
Virk v. Brar
,

2012 BCSC 1004
at paras.
69-70
.

[62] A pleading can be embarrassing if it
does not state the real issue in an intelligible form. It can also be
embarrassing if it is prolix, includes irrelevant facts, argument or evidence.
It can be prejudicial if it is designed to or has the effect of confusing the
defendant, making it difficult, if not impossible, to answer;
Virk
at para.
75
.

[63] These same
concerns can constitute an abuse of the court if a litigant has been expressly
told that there are aspects of its pleadings that are deficient or defective,
and if that litigant persists, in its amended claim, to advance the same claims
or issues in the same way

[
19
]

In addition, courts dealing with applications to
strike must also be mindful of whether the defective pleadings can be cured by
amendment: see para. 25 of
Wong v. Wilson
,
2013 BCSC 1465
. I
agree with the defendants’ submission that it is not the court’s role to
articulate for a litigant a comprehensible and legally cognizable cause of
action. To that end, I am guided by the observation of Donald J.A. in
The

Owners, Strata Plan LMS 3259 v. Sze Holdings Inc.
,
2015 BCCA 424
at
para.
11
, where he states:

[11]      … Self-represented
litigants must understand that the court is not a free fire zone where anything
can be said regardless of the harm to others and their reputations.

[
20
]

However, I must also consider, as the defendants have demonstrated
on this application, that the courts must be vigilant to ensure fairness to
self-represented litigants. While this may include a margin of lenience, the
fact that a litigant is self-represented does not relieve them of the
obligation to comply with the Rules and with orders made by the court: see
Nayyar
v. Performance Realty Ltd.
,
2012 BCSC 1798
at para.
27
.

[
21
]

Relevant to this point is the recent decision of

Beach Estate v. Beach
,
2019 BCCA 277
where Chief Justice Baumann stated
this at para. 68:

. . . It is not disputed that the judge was
correct in finding Nancy’s pleading in respect of the Settlement Agreement
inadequate and defective. Nor is it disputed that the judge correctly reached
the same conclusion concerning the amended pleading Nancy proffered at the
hearing. However, it seems to me that in the situation of a defective pleading
on an issue that noes not reach the “no triable issue” threshold, in a claim
brought by a self-represented litigant (at least), the proper course would be
to strike the pleading and permit the litigant to seek appropriate amendments.
This is the practice in the Supreme Court in these matters.

[Citations omitted.]

IV.

ANALYSIS

[
22
]

I start with what became obvious to me during the course of the
defendants’ submissions and having read the comprehensive material filed by the
defendants: This has been taxing litigation. The ANOCC contains many offensive
and improper assertions. I must also consider the interests of the individual
police officers who remain named in this lawsuit. Having heard Mr. Butcher’s
thoughtful submission about the deficiencies, M.P.W. sought to do better. He
agreed that he would not seek to advance much of the information contained in
the ANOCC. To that end, M.P.W. sought to deliver a more concise pleading after
removing many of the offensive paragraphs.

[
23
]

I agree with the defendants that granting the order I did provided M.P.W.
with a second chance to fix the pleading after already being provided with
guidance from the court two years prior. However, in light of the Further ANOCC,
which is a much streamlined pleading and having considered the authorities
governing pleadings (in particular, regarding cases involving self-represented
litigants), I am of the view that the Further ANOCC is a manageable document (subject
to the further revisions set out below), which will allow the defendants to
proceed to finality once and for all.

[
24
]

In response to the Further ANOCC, the defendants delivered a
response setting out further areas of deficiencies. In light of those
submissions and the plaintiff’s position, I agree that the Further ANOCC be
revised as follows:

a)

Para. 1(d) is not permitted and will be struck;

b)

Para. (1)(p) is not permitted and will be
struck;

c)

Under Part 1, para. 2 – the phrase “loss of
work” will be struck;

d)

Under Part 2, para. 2 – anything dealing
with pecuniary loss (including the reference to $500,000) will be struck;

e)

Under part 2, para. 4 – the phrase “The
plaintiff claims aggravated damages” will remain and everything else is struck;
and

f)

Under part 3, para. (1)(e) is struck.

V.

ORDER

[
25
]

In the result, I grant the following orders:

a)

The defendants’ application to strike the ANOCC
is granted;

b)

Leave is granted to the plaintiff to file the
Further ANOCC as revised in accordance with these reasons;

c)

The plaintiff must file the Further ANOCC as
revised by August 29, 2019; and

d)

Costs of this application to the defendants in
any event of the cause.

[
26
]

I wish to thank counsel for the professionalism they demonstrated
during the course of this application.

“Winteringham J.”
